title: Computer-Use Agents Learn When to Click and When to Script
dek: A new desktop agent trains clicks and code into one policy. Here is how that works, what it scored, and where agents still stall.
by: Draft for team review · written by Claude Code from published research and engineering writing · checked in code
lead: What is a computer use agent? A model that runs a computer through screenshots and actions. The newest learn when to click and when to run code, but hand-offs and specialist software still trip them.

cover.alt: One policy reads the screen and the task, then picks a GUI action or a code action; an evaluator checks the final state.
cover.caption: A hybrid computer-use agent picks a click or a script at each step, and only the end state is graded.

description: What is a computer use agent? A model that runs a computer through its screen. See how clicks, code and RL training fit together.
keywords: what is a computer use agent
decisions: Give an agent clicks and code only if it was trained to choose between them.
Grade agent tasks by the final machine state, not by the route taken.
Weigh RL updates per action step when actions differ a lot in length.
Make agents check sub-agent reports against the screen.
Test that agents release locks and hand off work when they finish.

items.question: Why did the OS-Helix team train the choice between clicks and code into the model?
options: Prompts cannot describe any tools to a model
Adding a code tool through the prompt made a GUI agent worse in their early tests
Code actions are forbidden on Ubuntu desktops
items.explanation: Their early experiments showed a GUI agent got worse when a code tool was simply added, so they made the routing a learned skill.

items.question: What does an OS-Helix task evaluator look at?
options: How many clicks the agent made
That the agent avoided writing code
The final state the machine ends in
items.explanation: The evaluator inspects the end state, so a solution built from clicks and one built from a script can be graded the same way.

items.question: What problem does balancing the RL update by action step solve?
options: Long code actions drowning out the signal from short clicks
The need for any evaluator during training
items.explanation: Counting per token lets long scripts dominate; counting per step gives each action one share of the update.

items.question: Which pattern did the CLASHarness benchmark report?
options: Stronger models followed misleading sub-agents more often
Finding an inconsistency was easier than fixing the system state
items.explanation: Agents could often spot a conflict, but repairing the state cost them task success, and closing actions failed most.

body.text: A computer-use agent drives the screen like a remote helper

body: A computer use agent is a model that runs a computer through its screen, like a remote helper borrowing your mouse. It sees what you would see. Then it clicks, types and scrolls. Teams build these agents on vision-language models, or VLMs, which take in images and text together [3]. The appeal is reach. Any app with a window becomes something the model can use.

The loop is simple to state. The agent captures a screenshot of the current desktop. The model reads it next to the task and emits one action, such as a click at a point or a keystroke. The computer changes, a fresh screenshot arrives, and the cycle repeats. The full record of screens and actions is a trajectory, and evaluation harnesses log it for later study [3].

Where does it break? A screen is a slow, narrow window onto a computer. The OS-Helix authors argue that real desktop work also means handling files, scripts and system state efficiently [1]. That tension drives the paper we follow through this post. It is a new arXiv study of an agent that mixes clicking with code [1].

body.caption: The basic loop a computer-use agent runs, one action per turn.
steps: Capture a screenshot of the desktop
Model reads the screen and the task
Model emits one action: click, type or code
An evaluator checks the final state

body.text: Clicks and code belong in one action space

body: The OS-Helix team starts from a blunt observation. Desktop work mixes reading an interface with changing things underneath it [1]. Renaming a whole folder of photos takes endless clicks, and a short script does it in one go. Checking that a chart looks right needs eyes, not code. A useful agent needs both moves.

So why not hand a GUI agent, one that works a graphical user interface, a code tool and let it choose? The team tried exactly that in early experiments. The agent got worse [1]. Their reading is that picking between clicks and code cannot be bolted on through the prompt. It has to be learned from training data that mixes both kinds of action [1].

body.text: In our preliminary experiments, naively adding a code tool degrades a GUI agent, revealing that GUI/code routing must be internalized through training on high-quality hybrid data.

body: OS-Helix therefore puts GUI actions and code execution into a single action space, the menu of moves a model can pick from at each step [1]. One policy, the trained model that maps a screen to an action, makes every choice. In our view, this is the right call. A prompt can list tools, but it cannot teach timing, and timing is the whole skill here.

body.text: Verifiable tasks come before any training run

body: A hybrid agent needs examples of hybrid work, and those are scarce. The team built them by pairing desktop applications with authentic files, a step it calls application-artifact composition [1]. Each pairing becomes a runnable Ubuntu state [1]. Picture a spreadsheet app opened on a genuine spreadsheet, not an empty window.

body.alt: Apps paired with real files make Ubuntu states; tasks and evaluators are written apart; SFT then online RL train the policy.
body.caption: OS-Helix builds checkable tasks first, then trains with a cold start and step-balanced online RL.

body: Next comes the clever part. Separate pipelines write the instruction and the evaluator, the code that inspects the final state [1]. The evaluator only looks at where the machine ended up. So it does not care if the agent clicked or scripted its way there [1]. That is what makes mixed solutions gradable at scale.

Training then runs in two phases [1]. Supervised fine-tuning, or SFT, on filtered hybrid data gives the policy a cold start. Online reinforcement learning, or RL, follows inside live desktop environments [1]. In RL the model improves from rewards on its own attempts, which are called rollouts.

The RL step hides a subtle trap. Clicks are short in tokens, while a code action can run long. Weigh every token equally and long scripts swamp the signal from clicks. The team's fix, Step-balanced GSPO, sums the importance weight per action step instead of per raw token [1]. An importance weight is the correction that rescales a sample drawn from an older policy.

body.label: Illustrative pattern: weighting an RL update by step instead of by token

body.text: OSWorld results put the trained agent at 66.44% success

body: So how well does it work? The team reports results on OSWorld-Verified, a desktop benchmark [1]. OS-Helix-27B and OS-Helix-35B-A3B beat their matched Qwen3.5 hybrid baselines by 35.0% and 33.7%, in relative terms [1]. The RL-trained 27B model then improves by 42.9% and reaches 66.44% success [1].

Read those numbers with care. A relative improvement is measured against the baseline's own score. It is not the same thing as percentage points. Of the figures above, only 66.44% is a plain success rate [1]. The paper's summary leaves out the baselines' own scores, so the gains cannot be turned into points here. We think that gap matters, because a big relative gain on a weak baseline can still leave a low score.

Ablations are experiments that remove one ingredient at a time. Here they point the same way, crediting learned coordination, verifiable supervision and step-balanced optimisation [1]. The team also reports cross-platform transfer to WindowsAgentArena, a Windows test bed [1]. We read the transfer as the strongest hint that the routing skill is real, not a quirk of one test.

body.caption: OS-Helix results on OSWorld-Verified as the authors report them.

body.text: Other agents can feed a computer-use agent stale facts

body: Real deployments rarely run one agent alone. A second paper, CLASHarness, tests what happens when peers disagree [2]. Sub-agents may report an outdated state, give clashing orders, or fight over shared files and permissions [2]. Its benchmark holds 600 multi-round tasks built around such conflicts [2].

body.alt: Three stages of a conflict: spot it, fix the state, close up. Closing up is where the most failures land.
body.caption: In multi-agent conflicts, the last step of releasing locks and handing off work fails most often.

body.text: Third, coordination protocols remain a universal bottleneck: even frontier models fail over 58% of closing actions, often forgetting to release shared locks or hand off tasks.

body: The construction matters for trusting the scores. The pipeline fixes the decisive visual facts before it renders a scene [2]. It then compiles code and semantic graders from reference runs that were actually executed. That makes every task solvable by design [2]. Free-form LLM generation, the authors warn, drifts and leaks answers instead [2].

Across 15 frontier models, three weak spots showed up [2]. Weaker models followed misleading sub-agent reports, and stronger ones checked the screen for themselves [2]. Spotting an inconsistency proved easier than repairing the system state [2]. Closing up was worst of all. Even frontier models failed over 58% of closing actions, such as releasing a shared lock [2].

We think the closing-action result is the one to take home. An agent that finishes the work but never hands it back leaves a mess for the next agent. Your harness should check that release step on its own, not assume it.

body.text: Scientific software marks where today's agents stall

body: Specialist tools are a harder test. OSWorld-Science gives agents 146 tasks in scientific software, from molecule drawing to pathology images, statistics and physics simulation [3]. Experts proposed the tasks. Execution-based evaluators inspect the outputs, such as segmentation masks and plots, and give partial credit for incomplete work [3].

The verdict is sobering. Across 12 VLMs, the authors found that even the strongest current models, run in a strong harness, still struggle with key scientific questions [3]. They also studied language, reasoning effort and context length as factors [3]. A good harness, it seems, cannot paper over an unfamiliar interface.

So where does the hybrid idea stop? It helps on desktop chores with a checkable end state [1]. It says little about hand-offs between agents or about specialist screens, where fresh failures show up [2, 3]. Nobody has yet reported how these agents fare on your own apps. To try one, start with tasks whose final state a script can verify, and read the CLASHarness paper before you add a second agent.
what is a computer use agent?

A computer use agent is an AI model that operates a computer through its screen, clicking, typing and scrolling like a person. It is usually built on a vision-language model, which reads screenshots and text together [3]. Newer agents such as OS-Helix can also run code in the same action space, choosing at each step between a click and a script [1].
how do computer use agents work?

They run a loop of seeing and acting. Each turn, the model reads a screenshot and the task, then emits one action, such as a click or a keystroke. The screen changes and the loop repeats until the task ends. Benchmarks log each run as a trajectory and check the final state of the machine [1, 3].
are computer use agents reliable yet?

Not for every job yet. On OSWorld-Verified, the RL-trained OS-Helix model reached 66.44% success [1]. In a multi-agent conflict benchmark, even frontier models failed over 58% of closing actions, such as releasing shared locks [2]. Scientific software also remains hard for current models, even inside a strong harness [3].
